    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-26-01204 / USCOURTS-ca6-26-01204-0

    FAPD-AI: In an opinion not recommended for publication, the Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment to Walmart, Inc. and Sam's Club on Steven Campbell's Title VII and Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act claims alleging race discrimination, hostile work environment, retaliation, and constructive discharge. The opinion holds that Campbell did not establish a prima facie case on his adverse-action claims, reasoning that he was not qualified for the promotions he sought and that his transfer to Medina was not an adverse action because he had requested it. It also treats his FMLA interference claim as forfeited for failure to develop the argument in his opening brief.   • Observed at 15:38:41 Eastern time ET
    Jacob Baxter v. Danny Cheadle, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-26-01199 / USCOURTS-ca7-26-01199-0

    FAPD-AI: The Seventh Circuit vacated the district court's dismissal of Jacob Baxter's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit against Village of Palestine Police Chief Danny Cheadle and remanded the case. The court held that the right of a for-cause public employee to a hearing before termination has been clearly established since Board of Regents v. Roth and Perry v. Sindermann, so Cheadle was not entitled to qualified immunity on that basis. The court directed the district court to determine on remand whether the Village adopted Division 2.1 of the Illinois Municipal Code (65 ILCS 5/10-2.1), which governs whether the for-cause protection applies. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Jeremy Haar v. Scott Moats, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-24-03140 / USCOURTS-ca7-24-03140-0

    FAPD-AI: In a nonprecedential order, the Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for prison medical officials in Jeremy Haar's Bivens action, holding that Haar did not exhaust Bureau of Prisons administrative remedies as required by 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a) before filing suit. The court stated that a warden's untimely response may be treated as a denial under 28 C.F.R. § 542.18, that the PLRA contains no futility exception, and that the district judge did not abuse her discretion in denying counsel. The court found the record did not show that the alleged statements by a health services administrator made the administrative process unavailable. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:40 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Jeremy Lewis (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-02365 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-02365-0

    FAPD-AI: The Seventh Circuit affirmed the judgment in United States v. Jeremy Don William Lewis, rejecting Lewis's appeal of his guilty plea to conspiracy to distribute more than 500 grams of methamphetamine. Lewis argued that the factual basis was insufficient and that he was not properly informed of the mandatory minimum sentence. The district court sentenced Lewis to 120 months' imprisonment under a Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(c)(1)(C) plea agreement. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:40 Eastern time ET
    John Johnson v. Wexford Health Sources, Inc., et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-26-01094 / USCOURTS-ca7-26-01094-0

    FAPD-AI: In a nonprecedential order, the Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the individual medical providers and for Wexford Health Sources, Inc. in John F. Johnson's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 action alleging failure to timely diagnose and treat deep vein thrombosis. The court found the record showed the providers evaluated, referred, treated, and monitored Johnson, and that Johnson offered no evidence of an express policy or widespread custom supporting his Monell claim against Wexford. The court also upheld the district court's denial of leave to file a surreply under C.D. Ill. R. 7.1(D)(2). USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:39 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Torres (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-40675 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-40675-0

    FAPD-AI: In United States v. Torres, the Fifth Circuit remanded a case in which the defendant, charged under 18 U.S.C. § 2251(a) and § 2252A(a)(5)(B), had a magistrate judge's pretrial release order revoked, and the district court deferred a detention hearing until after a competency examination. The panel stated that the Bail Reform Act requires a hearing under 18 U.S.C. § 3142(f) and found no textual support for the district court's deferral, while leaving the revocation orders in place pending that hearing. The district court may hold the detention hearing within three days after the examiner's report is filed, which is expected by December 6. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-60105 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-60105-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated November 24, 2026, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the Northern District of Mississippi's dismissal for failure to state a claim of Rebecca Lynn Bumgardner's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 complaint against county sheriff's office officials.     FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated November 24, 2026, the Fifth Circuit summarily affirmed the Southern District of Mississippi judgment in United States v. Corey Pendleton as to his Second Amendment challenges to 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), citing circuit precedent. The court dismissed the appeal as to his Commerce Clause challenge because the challenge falls within the appeal waiver in his plea agreement and is not covered by the Bruen carveout.     Vargas Mares v. Blanche (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-60277 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-60277-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated November 24, 2026, the Fifth Circuit denied Sergio Vargas Mares's petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision affirming the denial of cancellation of removal. The court stated that it lacks jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) to review the agency's factual hardship findings, but has jurisdiction under § 1252(a)(2)(D) to review whether established facts satisfy the legal standard, and it also denied the Government's motion for summary disposition or an extension of time. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-10969 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-10969-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal of Marlene Evans's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 complaint, which challenged a Rockdale County, Georgia state-court order requiring her to obtain leave before filing new lawsuits, on the ground that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine deprived the district court of subject-matter jurisdiction. The court reasoned that the requested injunctive relief would require vacatur of the state-court judgment and that the damages claims challenged the issuance of that judgment. The court modified the dismissal to be without prejudice and affirmed the order as modified, declining to reach the judicial immunity question. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:30 Eastern time ET
    Jesus Valle v. Orange County Housing and Community Development Di, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-13501 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-13501-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit dismissed sua sponte Jesus de Israel Valle's appeal from a September 25, 2026 case management and scheduling order in his action against the Orange County Housing and Community Development Division and two employees, for lack of appellate jurisdiction. The court stated that the order was not a final decision under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and was not appealable under the collateral order doctrine. All pending motions were denied as moot. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:29 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Hernan Mojica-Renteria (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-10896 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-10896-0

    FAPD-AI: In United States v. Mojica-Renteria, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of a motion for sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A) and U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6), filed by a defendant serving a 292-month sentence. The court held that the district court did not abuse its discretion in concluding that the 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) factors weighed against a reduction, and that this determination was a sufficient basis for denying the motion. The opinion addresses the defendant's arguments that the district court made a legal error in weighing those factors and failed to explain its ruling adequately. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:29 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Eber Lopez (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12877 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12877-0

    FAPD-AI: In the unpublished per curiam opinion in USA v. Eber Lopez, the Eleventh Circuit addressed a defendant's appeal of his convictions and 327-month sentence for conspiracy to distribute cocaine and possession with intent to distribute cocaine. The court held that the defendant waived his challenge to a prior conviction's serious drug felony status by failing to respond to the government's 21 U.S.C. § 851 notice, and that his plea agreement admission made a specific finding unnecessary. The court also found the plea colloquy sufficient under Rule 11 and stated that it affirmed in part and dismissed in part. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:29 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Kevin Campos Rivera (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12917 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12917-0

    FAPD-AI: In the unpublished per curiam order in USA v. Kevin Campos Rivera, the Eleventh Circuit granted the government's motion to dismiss the appeal as barred by the appeal waiver in the defendant's plea agreement. The order cites United States v. Bushert, United States v. Grinard-Henry, and Hunter v. United States, 608 U.S. 713 (2026), for the principles that knowing and voluntary sentence appeal waivers are enforceable and that a waiver may be set aside only where the sentence reflects egregious error that would bring the judicial system into disrepute. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:29 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Delta Rushing, II (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13570 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13570-0

    FAPD-AI: In the unpublished per curiam opinion in USA v. Delta Rushing, II, the Eleventh Circuit granted the government's motion for summary reversal, vacated the defendant's sentence, and remanded for a new sentencing hearing. The court held that the district court plainly erred in applying the repeat and dangerous sex offender enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.5 based on a prior conviction under Fla. Stat. § 847.0135(4), which it determined is not a categorical sex offense under United States v. Lusk. The opinion states that on resentencing the district court is not limited to correcting that error. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:38:29 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Damion Lovelady (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13666 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13666-0

    FAPD-AI: In the unpublished per curiam opinion in USA v. Damion Lovelady, the Eleventh Circuit addressed a 110-month sentence for possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and stated that it affirmed in part and vacated and remanded in part. The court held that Georgia aggravated assault convictions were properly treated as crimes of violence under U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(a)(2), as foreclosed by United States v. Hicks and United States v. Morales-Alonso, and that facts in the presentence report to which the defendant did not object were admitted for sentencing purposes. The opinion also addresses the four-level enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B), though the provided text is truncated before the court's ruling on that enhancement. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-10870 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-10870-0

    FAPD-AI: In MedEnvios Healthcare, Inc. v. Secretary, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment upholding two Medicare audits that found a medical device supplier needed to repay approximately $2.5 million. The court held that neither the Constitution nor the governing statute required the Medicare auditors to include zero-paid claims in the claims analyzed through extrapolation. The opinion also rejected the supplier's remaining arguments, including its challenge to the disclosure of the universe of claims considered. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    119 HR 10234 RH: Consumer-Led Enhancement of Annuity and insurance Registration Forms Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr10234rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, titled the Consumer-Led Enhancement of Annuity and insurance Registration Forms Act or the CLEAR Forms Act, would add section 6A to the Securities Act of 1933, defining covered insurance contracts such as contingent deferred annuities and registered index-linked life insurance. It directs the Securities and Exchange Commission to propose rules within 12 months and finalize them within 30 months of enactment to establish registration forms for these contracts, including investor testing for contingent deferred annuities. If the rules are not finalized within 36 months, those contracts may be registered on existing forms specified in the bill until the Commission finalizes the rules. BILLS-SEL-01

    119 HR 1653 RH: Civil Investigative Demand Reform Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr1653rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, titled the Civil Investigative Demand Reform Act of 2026, amends section 1052 of the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 to limit civil investigative demands to violations occurring within 6 years and to require that demands include specific reference to particular facts. It allows an attorney advising a recipient to submit questions to the Bureau, sets response and return-date timing for those questions, and extends confidential treatment to petitions submitted to the Bureau. The bill also expands the grounds for setting aside a demand to include constitutional or legal rights and burdensome or duplicative demands, and makes the Bureau's denial of a petition to modify or set aside a demand subject to judicial review. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 01:55:42 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 4936 RH: Taskforce for Recognizing and Averting Payment Scams Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr4936rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, titled the Taskforce for Recognizing and Averting Payment Scams Act or the TRAPS Act, directs the Secretary of the Treasury to establish within 90 days a Task Force for Recognizing and Averting Payment Scams. The Task Force's membership includes specified federal officials, along with appointed representatives from financial institutions, digital payment networks, consumer protection organizations, and other stakeholders, and it is required to meet at least three times in the first year after enactment. The Task Force must submit a report with strategic and legislative recommendations within one year of its establishment, provide annual updates, and terminate 3 years after it submits that initial report. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 01:55:42 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 5889 RH: Eviction Helpline Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr5889rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, titled the Eviction Helpline Act, directs the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development to establish within 1 year of enactment a hotline that provides tenants of covered federally assisted rental dwelling units with counseling, resources, and referrals related to eviction. The bill requires that information about the hotline be published in common areas of federally assisted rental dwellings and through other means the Secretary determines appropriate. Covered units are defined by reference to specified HUD assistance programs and to properties with federally backed mortgage loans, and the program terminates 7 years after enactment. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 01:55:42 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 7030 RH: Securing Facilities for Mental Health Services Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr7030rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, titled the Securing Facilities for Mental Health Services Act, amends section 242(b)(1) of the National Housing Act by striking subparagraph (B) and redesignating subparagraph (C) as subparagraph (B), which provides parity for licensed hospitals in access to the hospital mortgage insurance program. The amendments apply for the period beginning 9 months after enactment and ending 5 years after enactment. The bill also requires the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development to submit a report to the House Committee on Financial Services and the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs within 5 years of enactment assessing the results and effectiveness of the program expansion. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 01:55:42 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 7866 RH: American Lending Fairness Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr7866rh

    FAPD-AI: The reported bill, titled the American Lending Fairness Act of 2026, amends section 27 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act and section 205(g) of the Federal Credit Union Act so that, if a State adopts a law or certifies voter approval stating that the State does not want the federal interest rate exportation provisions to apply to loans made by its chartered institutions, those provisions will not apply to such loans made after that date. The bill repeals section 525 of the Depository Institutions Deregulation and Monetary Control Act of 1980. It also provides that the amendments govern the legal effect of any State law adopted or certification made under section 525 before the date of enactment. BILLS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 01:55:42 Eastern time ET
    119 HR 8957 RH: American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8957rh

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8957, the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, as reported by the House Committee on Financial Services with amendments, would direct the Secretary of the Treasury to establish a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a Digital Asset Stockpile within the Department of the Treasury no later than 180 days after enactment, for the custody of qualifying Bitcoin and other qualifying digital assets owned by the Federal Government. It requires annual reports to the House Financial Services and Senate Banking Committees, security measures, transfer of qualifying assets to Treasury title, and sales of reserve Bitcoin only under a Treasury rule, and it bars sale of digital assets resulting from a fork or airdrop for one year. The text as provided is truncated before the remaining provisions. BILLS-SEL-01

(Pilatus) Model PC-6, PC-6-H1, PC-6-H2, PC-6/350, PC-6/350-H1, PC-6/350-H2, PC-6/A, PC-6/A-H1, PC-6/A-H2, PC-6/B-H2, PC-6/B1-H2, PC-6/B2-H2, PC-6/B2-H4, PC-6/C-H2, and PC-6/C1-H2 airplanes.     Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR · FR-2026-11-25 / 2026-23968

    official summary: We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), propose to list the peppered shiner ( Miniellus perpallidus ), a fish species from southeast Oklahoma and southern Arkansas, as an endangered species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (Act). This determination also serves as our 12-month finding on a petition to list the peppered shiner. After a review of the best available scientific and commercial information, we find that listing the species is warranted. Accordingly, we propose to list the peppered shiner as an endangered species under the Act. If finalized as proposed, this rule would add this species to the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and extend the Act's protections to the species. FR-SEL-02

    official summary: We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), propose to list the Rio Grande shiner ( Notropis jemezanus ), a fish species from the Rio Grande Basin in New Mexico, Texas, and Mexico, as an endangered species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (Act). This determination also serves as our 12-month finding on a petition to list the Rio Grande shiner. After a review of the best scientific and commercial data available, we find that listing the species is warranted. If we finalize this rule as proposed, it would add this species to the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and extend the Act's protections to the species. We find that critical habitat for this species is not determinable at this time. FR-SEL-02

    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-11-25 / 2026-23985

    official summary: The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-19-04, which applies to all Airbus SAS Model A350-941 and -1041 airplanes. AD 2024-19-04 requires a one-time detailed inspection of the engine nacelle anti-icing (NAI) forward bulkhead locating holes for elongation and loose fasteners and applicable corrective actions and prohibits the installation of affected parts under certain conditions. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-19-04, it has been determined that affected parts must accumulate at least 2,000 flight cycles (FC) since installation prior to the inspection to ensure that the inspection will detect discrepancies. This proposed AD would continue to require the actions in AD 2024-19-04 and would amend the compliance time for the inspection. This proposed AD would also prohibit the installation of affected parts under certain conditions. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. FR-SEL-02

    official summary: The NCUA Board (Board) is issuing a final rule increasing two thresholds in its regulation implementing management official interlocks for purposes of the Depository Institution Management Interlocks Act (DIMIA). DIMIA authorizes NCUA to adjust the major assets prohibition thresholds through regulation to respond to inflation or market changes. This final rule increases both major assets prohibition thresholds to $10 billion to account for changes in the United States banking market since 1996. Additionally, the final rule removes a presumption related to depository institutions controlled or managed by persons who are members of a minority group or women. FR-SEL-01

The final rule also removes filing requirements related to a corporate credit union's annual report and any management letter or other report issued by its independent public accountant. The intended effect is to reduce unnecessary regulatory burden and provide corporate credit unions with greater flexibility. FR-SEL-01

    Federal Register · govinfo API · SURFACE TRANSPORTATION BOARD · FR-2026-11-25 / 2026-24003

    official summary: The Board partially grants a petition for rulemaking and proposes amendments to its regulations implementing section 208 of the National Trails System Act Amendments of 1983 to streamline the railbanking process. Under the proposal, the Board would no longer issue Notices or Certificates of Interim Trail Use during trail-use negotiations. Only after an agreement is reached would the Board issue an order authorizing transfer to the trail sponsor. Abandonment authority would no longer be prerequisite to railbanking. The Board would also confirm that by authorizing transfer the Board is not exercising any power of eminent domain or authorizing a taking. FR-SEL-02

    FAPD-AI: Proclamation 11082 of November 20, 2026, designates November 2026 as National Adoption Month and calls on Americans to ensure that every child has the love and support needed to live a long, healthy, and prosperous life. It describes Federal actions including expansion of the Adoption Tax Credit, the Fostering the Future for American Children and Families Executive Order, the Fostering the Future Accounts, and the launch of FosteringTheFuture.gov. It encourages faith-based organizations, houses of worship, businesses, nonprofits, and community groups to support adoptive families. FR-SEL-03

    Protecting the Executive's Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · FR-2026-11-25 / 2026-24114

    FAPD-AI: Executive Order 14439 of November 20, 2026, requires all Federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House and contracting agencies of any pending or future congressional request concerning their communications or work with the executive branch, and to follow instructions on withholding communications that the White House or an agency determines are protected by executive privilege. It directs agencies to coordinate with the White House and contractors on responses to such requests, directs the Office of Management and Budget to issue implementation guidance, and states that agencies shall consider actions including contract termination and debarment or suspension for noncompliance. The order also includes severability and general provisions stating that it creates no enforceable rights, and it provides that publication costs are borne by the Department of Labor. FR-SEL-03
